'''''Alocasia odora''''', also known as '''night-scented lily''', '''Asian taro''' or '''giant upright elephant ear''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Araceae|arum]] family native to [[East Asia|East]] and [[Southeast Asia]] (Japan, China, [[Indochina]], [[Assam]], Bangladesh, [[Borneo]], Taiwan).<ref name=parvati>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=6798 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref>{{TaiBNET| zh=姑-{}-婆-{}-芋 | id=201130 | binomial=Alocasia odora | authority=(Lodd.) Spach., 1846 | var= | access-date=2016-05-01}}</ref> Traditionally, ''A. odora'' is sometime used as a medicine for the treatment of the [[common cold]] in Vietnam.<ref>MATSUDA M and NAWATA E (2002) "Taro in Northern Vietnam : Its Uses, Cultivation, and Genetic Variation" Japanese Journal of Tropical Agriculture, 46/4, p.252</ref>

==Description==
This species of ''Alocasia'' grows to about 0.5–1.6 m high, or just over 5 feet, with corms measuring 4 cm to around 10 cm in diameter and 3–5 cm wide. The leaves are big, diamond-blade-shaped, slightly “teardrop” in form, but ovate, with a light green hue and a cordate base. The petioles are 0.3–1.0 m long, with the lower parts clasped around the stem.<ref>{{ cite book | first1=Yoshitaka | last1=Tanaka | first2=Nguyen | last2=Van Ke | date=2007 | title=Edible Wild Plants of Vietnam: The Bountiful Garden | publisher=Thailand: Orchid Press | isbn=978-9745240896 | page=29}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Alocasia odora'' leaves and stems are used as a green vegetable in the cuisines of [[Southeast Asia]], and often used to flavor soups or [[Stir frying|stir-fried]] dishes. The leaves and stems should not be consumed raw, nor should any of the green plant material. At certain Asian or specialty markets, it is usually peeled and boiled to be sold either frozen, bagged in its own liquids, or canned.

Nonetheless, the plant is actually inedible when raw, and may cause mild to significant gastrointestinal discomfort, due to the composition of its leaves, which are covered in microscopic, needle-shaped [[Ergastic substance#Crystals|raphide]]s (or [[calcium oxalate]] crystals).<ref>Jeong Mi Moon, et al. 'Toxicities of raw Alocasia odora', Human & Experimental Toxicology. [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21177728 Abstract]</ref> Consumption of undercooked [[Araceae|aroid]] leaves can result in several uncomfortable symptoms; side effects range from an itchy, sharp sensation in the esophagus, similar to a feeling of “broken glass” or sand being swallowed (usually lasting no more than several hours), to abdominal pain, hot and cold flashes, nausea and vomiting. However, similarly to another, more common ''taro'' plant, ''[[Colocasia esculenta]],'' the [[corm]] (root bulb) of ''A. odora'' is sometimes boiled and mashed like [[potato]]es. As with the green plant material, the corm should also not be consumed raw or undercooked. In Japan, there are several cases of [[food poisoning]] by accidental consumption. [[Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (Japan)|The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare]] warned not to eat ''A. odora'', which looks similar to edible ''[[Leucocasia gigantea]]'' or the aforementioned ''C. esculenta''.<ref>"[http://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNASDG0505P_W2A001C1CC0000/ 「クワズイモ」誤食に注意呼び掛け　厚労省 高知・四万十市で食中]". 日本経済新聞.</ref><ref>後藤勝実、月岡淳子. "[http://www.mhlw.go.jp/topics/syokuchu/poison/higher_det_05.html クワズイモ]". 自然毒のリスクプロファイル. 厚生労働省.</ref><ref>さいたま市保健福祉局 健康科学研究センター 生活科学課 (2012年11月19日). "{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130413141658/http://www.city.saitama.jp/www/contents/1350446407956/index.html|title=食べられないイモ『クワズイモ』}}". さいたま市.</ref>

Typical of leafy green vegetables—and despite its toxicity if prepared incorrectly—the leaves of this plant are rich in vitamins and minerals, including [[thiamin]], [[riboflavin]], [[iron]], [[phosphorus]] and [[zinc]]. Additionally, they are a very good source of [[Vitamin B6|vitamin B<sub>6</sub>]], [[vitamin C]], [[Vitamin B3|niacin]], [[potassium]], [[copper]], and [[manganese]]. Taro corms are very high in starch, while being somewhat less starchy than potatoes; the forms are a good source of [[dietary fiber]]. Like its stems and leaves, [[oxalic acid]] may yet be present in the corm, albeit in trace amounts.

== Taxonomy and etymology ==
''Alocasia odora'' is named ''odora'' because of the flowers that produce a fragrance which is especially strong at night. The scent is sometimes described as being ''pleasant'' and ''sweet''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wyatt |first=Sara |date=2022-10-08 |title=Alocasia Odora {{!}} Elephant Ear Plant Care Tips |url=https://plantsinsights.com/alocasia-odora/ |access-date=2023-10-28 |website=Plants Insights |language=en-US}}</ref>
